payload.viable_set:
KILLER. THREE viable candidates survive, and two of them are genuinely competitive rather than strawmen - which I can demonstrate rather than assert.

X1 'ripgrep + git, selectors' - 101 weighted.
X3 'git only, ZERO new dependencies' - 98 weighted.
X2 'ripgrep + git, semantic join' - 90 weighted, surviving on an untested assumption rather than on strength.

THE EVIDENCE THAT X3 IS NOT A STRAWMAN: I seeded it expecting the exercise to kill it. The killer example S1 slide 3 was run against it for real (run-115221d0d8fb) - `git grep -n -C 2 <pattern> main -- <path>` returned the match with two lines of context either side, prefixed ref:path:line. It passed on the first attempt. X3 now beats the leader on the owner's own most-repeated principles - zero dependencies, and ONE implementation for both tree and record where X1 needs two tools to answer one question.

And the DATUM IS DISQUALIFIED: today's surface fails the C2 REACH veto outright - it cannot reach refs or outside sources, so killer story S1 is impossible on it rather than merely slow. That matters for what this gate means: the question is no longer whether to act, it is which successor.

Six weighted points separate X1 from X3, which I would not defend as a real difference given that X1's decisive advantage (typed --json output) is scored from DOCUMENTATION, because rg is not installed on this machine and could not be exercised. That asymmetry in the evidence is exactly why convergence belongs at M5 behind a spike, not here.
payload.complete_allocation:
All 28 functions are allocated in every candidate; no function is unallocated and none is double-allocated.

SHARED ACROSS ALL THREE (the partitioning is candidate-independent): K2 HONESTY (F7-F9) allocates to the dispatch layer, deliberately ABOVE whichever search provider is chosen - so that refusal semantics cannot vary per provider, which is the defect that let a missing argument produce a confident search. K3 ALTERATION (F10-F13) allocates to the file lane. K4 SUPPLY (F14-F16) to the packet builder. K5 DECISION (F17-F21) to a lint registry keyed by check id on the machine-state node. K6 (F22-F25) to the close, (F26-F27) to se_config, (F28) to the call log.

WHERE THE CANDIDATES DIFFER - K1 RETRIEVAL only:
- X1/X2 split K1 across TWO providers behind one facade: rg serves F1/F2 over the tree, git serves F3/F4 over refs. INTERFACES: facade->rg (argv in, JSON events out, exit code), facade->git (argv in, text out), facade->caller (one normalized result shape). FOUR inter-cluster interfaces.
- X3 allocates all of K1 to ONE provider: git serves tree and refs alike. INTERFACES: facade->git, facade->caller. THREE interfaces, and one output shape to normalize instead of two.

RATIONALE RECORDED: X1/X2 accept an extra interface to gain typed output and native bounding; X3 accepts weaker output and manual bounding to gain a single path and no dependency. Both keep the K4-K5 contract edge intact - the constraint the partitioning named as load-bearing, that a rule supplied to the agent and a rule enforced by a lint must be the same rule.

ROW 6 differs too: X1/X3 allocate F14 to selector matching (machine-readable applies_to), X2 to semantic matching over the existing BM25 index. Same function, different mechanism, which is why it is a candidate axis rather than a detail.
payload.criteria_traced:
Eight criteria, every one carrying its requirement lineage and its weight's reasoning; the full derivation is at derive_criteria.

FROM REQUIREMENTS: C1 freshness <- R1,R3,R5. C2 reach <- R5,R6,R7. C4 structured output <- R3,R19,R28. C6 bounded cost <- R28. C7 selection correctness <- R14,R15. C8 migration debt <- R14.
FROM STAKEHOLDER TENSIONS AND OWNER RULINGS: C3 one-click install <- the owner's standing bar, restated at kickoff. C5 one implementation per job <- the owner's explicit no-duplicate-code ruling, and T4 (operator versus the no-fallback ruling) which is the tension it embodies.

TWO ARE VETOES RATHER THAN WEIGHTS, declared before scoring so they could not be traded away afterwards: C1 because a stale answer is a wrong answer wearing a confident face, and C2 because a working-tree-only tool fails the killer story absolutely rather than partially. C2 is what disqualified the datum.

C8's LOW WEIGHT (2) IS ITSELF A RECORDED DECISION, not an oversight: migrating ten nodes is cheap, and weighting migration highly would have picked the mechanism that fits today's accidental data over the one that is right.

FIVE CANDIDATE CRITERIA WERE PRUNED with reasons - raw speed, maturity, licence, multi-language extensibility, token efficiency - the last because it is an OUTCOME of C4 and C6 rather than an independent axis, and scoring it separately would double-count.
payload.front_recorded:
The front is {X1, X3, X2}, recorded honestly including the member that is weak.

X1 and X3 are genuinely non-dominated: X1 wins C4 and C6, X3 wins C3 and C5. Neither dominates the other, and the six-point gap is inside my own scoring noise.

X2 survives on a TECHNICALITY and I am naming it as such: it beats X1 only on C8 (weight 2) while losing C7 (weight 5). A bad trade, Pareto-legal. It stays for one reason - its weakness is an ASSUMPTION rather than a measurement. Nobody has tested whether BM25 over applies_to prose picks the rules that actually bind a state. If it picks well, its C7 score is wrong and it becomes the cheapest candidate by a distance; if badly, it is eliminated on evidence instead of on my prior.

EVERY ELIMINATION REASONED, at evaluate_set: the datum (C2 veto); index-based candidates zoekt/Sourcegraph/OpenGrok/embeddings (C1 veto, and independently C3 - the scan confirmed Sourcegraph indexes the default branch with others opt-in, the wrong default for a system whose evidence lives on non-default refs); ast-grep as a replacement (answers a question the register does not ask, retained as a later addition with a trigger); and eight row-level eliminations each with its reason.

ONE REVERSAL RECORDED: X3 was seeded expecting to be killed and survived the attempt. A candidate that survives an attempt on its life is stronger evidence than one that was never tested.
payload.feasibility_checked:
ROUGH CHECKS PER SURVIVOR, and the honest asymmetry between them is stated rather than smoothed.

X3 - FEASIBILITY PARTLY PROVEN, not estimated. git grep across a tag (run-6405dc1414a2), across v1's branch (same run), and with context over a ref (run-115221d0d8fb) all returned usable output on this machine, today. The unproven parts are bounded and known: parsing the `:` versus `-` separator safely on paths containing those characters; capping results and line width at our boundary since git grep offers neither; and the tracked-files-only default, which makes untracked work-in-progress invisible unless explicitly included. None of these is a research question.

X1/X2 - FEASIBILITY UNPROVEN ON THIS MACHINE, and that is the point. rg is not installed (P1), so nothing about the npm package's resolution, the binary's behaviour on Windows, or the --json event shape has been observed here. All three are documented and none is exotic, but 'documented' is exactly the standard of evidence this project got burned by twice this week - the design document said the hosted brief was built and verified, and it was not. Feasibility for X1/X2 therefore rests on an M5 spike, not on this state.

X2's EXTRA UNKNOWN: whether semantic matching selects the RIGHT rules. Not a feasibility question - it will certainly return something - but a correctness one, which is worse, because it fails silently by returning plausible rules rather than by erroring.

COMMON FEASIBILITY, all three: the lint registry, the verdict block, the annotated tags, branch deletion and se_config are ordinary engineering against surfaces we already own. The one shared unknown is whether the M4 element allocation is machine-readable enough for a models-adhered lint - named at gate_inputs, still unproven, and scheduled for M5 rather than assumed here.
